title: Instrument Rating (Airplane)
summary: A complete study path for the FAA Instrument Rating Airplane knowledge test and the knowledge portions of the practical test.
who: This course is for airplane pilots preparing to fly under IFR. It covers instrument procedures, weather, navigation, regulations, risk management and the aeronautical experience required by Part 61.

facts.label: Instrument training with an instructor
facts.value: 15 hours from an authorized instrument instructor

facts.label: Recent instrument experience
facts.value: Within 6 calendar months: 6 approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses

notes: An authorized instructor or approved course must endorse your preparation.
Use current charts and the FAA testing supplement while practicing.
A passing report does not replace the instructor endorsements and flight experience required for the practical test.
The examiner evaluates knowledge, risk management and flight skills through instrument tasks.
Use the ACS codes on your knowledge test report to target review before the practical test.

requirements.text: Hold at least a private pilot certificate, or apply for it with the instrument rating.
Complete and log the aeronautical knowledge and flight training required by 61.65.
Log 50 hours of cross-country time as pilot in command and 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time.
Complete the required 250 nautical mile IFR cross-country with approaches at each airport and three different kinds of approaches.

plan.focus: Build instrument scan, systems and regulation fundamentals.
Read clearances, charts and navigation systems as one connected route.
Practice departures, arrivals, holding and approaches.
Finish weather, icing, emergencies and decision making, then use the Aha game for review.

test_day: Bring acceptable identification and the required endorsement.
Use the supplied testing supplement and verify every chart scale and legend.
Write clear notes for holding entries, wind corrections and approach questions.
Keep the Airman Knowledge Test Report for your instructor and examiner.
after: Review each missed ACS code with an instrument instructor.
Complete the experience and recent practical-test preparation in 61.65.
Fly realistic scenarios that join weather, clearances, navigation and missed approaches.
Use the current Instrument Rating Airplane ACS for oral and flight preparation.

modules.title: Eligibility, experience and IFR privileges
modules.summary: Understand what the rating permits and what experience must be logged before the practical test.
objectives: Separate rating requirements from instrument currency.

sections.heading: Eligibility and training
points: Section 61.65 requires the appropriate pilot certificate, English proficiency, ground training, flight training, a knowledge test and a practical test.

For airplanes, the aeronautical experience includes 50 hours of cross-country pilot-in-command time, 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time and 15 hours with an authorized instrument instructor.

sections.heading: Privileges and currency
points: An instrument rating lets a properly qualified pilot operate under IFR and in weather below VFR minimums. The aircraft, equipment, inspections and operation must also qualify.
The rating never expires, but recent instrument experience does. Section 61.57 governs currency, and an instrument proficiency check is required after the allowed reestablishment period.

numbers.value: 3 hours within the 2 calendar months before the test month

traps: Instrument currency is not the same as an instrument rating.
The 50 cross-country hours are pilot-in-command time, not simply all cross-country time.

check.q: How much cross-country pilot-in-command time does 61.65(d) require?
check.why: The airplane instrument-rating requirement is 50 hours of cross-country time as pilot in command, including 10 hours in airplanes.

check.q: How much instrument time is required for the airplane rating?
check.why: Section 61.65(d) requires 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time.

check.q: Does an instrument rating expire when recent instrument experience lapses?
choices: No, but IFR privileges require currency
check.why: The rating remains on the certificate, but the pilot must meet 61.57 before acting as pilot in command under IFR or below VFR minimums.

modules.title: Flight instruments and attitude instrument flying
modules.summary: Connect instrument-system behavior to a stable scan and reliable aircraft control.

sections.heading: Instrument systems
points: The airspeed indicator uses pitot and static pressure. The altimeter and vertical-speed indicator use static pressure. Blockages produce different errors depending on which source is blocked.
Electronic flight displays use sensors and computers, but they still require cross-checking. Compare independent sources before trusting a surprising indication.

sections.heading: Scan and control
points: Attitude instrument flying uses a continuous cross-check, interpretation and control process. Fixation, omission and emphasis are common scan errors.
Use small corrections, trim the airplane and confirm the trend. Partial-panel flying demands a simpler scan and disciplined use of the instruments that remain reliable.

numbers.value: Within 75 feet of a known elevation

traps: A frozen pitot tube and blocked drain can make indicated airspeed behave like an altimeter.
A failed attitude source may look believable during a slow divergence.

check.q: Which instruments use only static pressure?
check.why: The altimeter and vertical-speed indicator are static-system instruments.

check.q: What is fixation in an instrument scan?
choices: Staring too long at one instrument
Scanning too quickly to read anything
check.why: Fixation is concentrating on one instrument at the expense of the rest of the cross-check.

check.q: What is the best response to one unexpected indication?
choices: Make a large immediate control input
check.why: Cross-checking independent sources helps distinguish aircraft motion from an instrument failure.

modules.title: IFR rules, clearances and flight plans
modules.summary: Apply the operating rules and turn an ATC clearance into an accurate plan.
objectives: Identify required IFR equipment and inspections.

sections.heading: Aircraft and preflight
points: Section 91.205 lists equipment required for IFR. Sections 91.411 and 91.413 set inspection intervals for altimeter/static systems and transponders.
IFR preflight planning includes weather, fuel, alternatives, delays, runway data and procedures. The filed flight plan is a request; the clearance is the authorization.

sections.heading: Clearances and lost communications
points: Copy route, altitude, departure frequency and transponder code in a consistent order. Read back hold-short instructions, runway assignments and items ATC requests.
Under 91.185, use the route priority assigned, vectored, expected, then filed. Use the highest applicable altitude among the minimum IFR altitude, expected altitude and last assigned altitude.

traps: A filed altitude does not override an assigned altitude.
Lost-communications rules do not require remaining airborne when a safe VFR landing is possible under 91.185(b).

check.q: Which item is part of the usual CRAFT clearance-copy sequence?
check.why: CRAFT ends with transponder code after clearance limit, route, altitude and departure frequency.

check.q: What is first in the 91.185 lost-communications route priority?
check.why: Use the route assigned in the last ATC clearance before considering vectored, expected or filed routes.

check.q: How often is the IFR altimeter and static-system inspection normally required?
check.why: Section 91.411 sets a 24-calendar-month interval.

modules.title: Enroute charts, navigation and altitude
modules.summary: Use charts, navigation systems and altitude rules to remain protected throughout an IFR route.
objectives: Choose legal and practical IFR altitudes.

sections.heading: Routes and altitudes
points: Low enroute charts depict airways, fixes, navigation facilities, changeover points and published altitudes. Read every legend and note before relying on a symbol.
The MEA supports obstacle clearance and acceptable navigation signal coverage. Other published altitudes, such as MOCA, MRA and MCA, answer different questions.

sections.heading: Navigation integrity
points: VOR use under IFR requires the check or inspection in 91.171. Record the date, place, bearing error and signature for an operational check.
GPS operations depend on approved equipment, current data and integrity monitoring. Know what the unit annunciates when integrity is unavailable and what alternate means the operation requires.

numbers.value: 1,000 feet; 2,000 feet in designated mountainous areas

traps: MOCA navigation-signal coverage is normally assured only within 22 nautical miles of a VOR.
An RNAV fix name does not by itself prove the aircraft is approved for the procedure.

check.q: How recently must a VOR have been checked before IFR use?
check.why: Section 91.171 requires the VOR equipment to have been checked within the preceding 30 days.

check.q: What does an MEA primarily provide?
check.why: The minimum enroute altitude supplies obstacle clearance and acceptable navigation-signal coverage along the route segment.

check.q: What must a pilot do when a GPS reports lost integrity for a procedure that needs it?
choices: Continue because the route is loaded
Use an approved alternative or discontinue the procedure
Cycle the unit until the warning clears
check.why: A pilot may not rely on navigation guidance when required integrity is unavailable.

modules.title: Departures, arrivals and holding
modules.summary: Plan transitions between terminal and enroute flight without losing terrain or traffic protection.
objectives: Use obstacle departure and arrival procedures.
Correct entries and timing for wind.

sections.heading: Departures and arrivals
points: Obstacle departure procedures provide obstacle clearance when flown as published. Standard instrument departures also organize traffic and require an ATC clearance unless assigned as part of the clearance.
Arrival procedures connect the enroute structure to terminal operations. Check altitude, speed and navigation requirements before accepting one.

sections.heading: Holding
points: A holding clearance includes the fix, direction, radial or course, leg length when needed, turn direction and expect-further-clearance time. Ask when any element is unclear.
Entries are recommended techniques, not regulatory boundaries. Prioritize remaining in protected airspace, then adjust heading and timing for wind.

numbers.item: Standard holding leg at or below 14,000 feet MSL
Standard holding leg above 14,000 feet MSL

numbers.value: Right turns unless published or assigned otherwise

traps: A diverse vector area is not an obstacle departure procedure.
Time the outbound leg to produce the correct inbound time after wind correction.

check.q: What is the standard holding turn direction unless otherwise published or assigned?
check.why: Standard holding patterns use right turns.

check.q: What is the standard inbound leg time at 10,000 feet MSL?
check.why: At or below 14,000 feet MSL, standard holding uses a one-minute inbound leg.

check.q: What is the first priority in choosing a holding entry?
check.why: Entry guidance supports the real objective: staying within the holding pattern's protected airspace.

modules.title: Instrument approaches and missed approaches
modules.summary: Read an approach chart from briefing strip through landing or missed approach.

sections.heading: Approach setup
points: Confirm chart date, procedure and runway, then brief navigation, frequencies, courses, altitudes, minimums, missed approach and relevant notes. Verify the loaded procedure against the chart.
A precision or approach-with-vertical-guidance procedure commonly uses a decision altitude. A nonprecision approach commonly uses a minimum descent altitude and a missed approach point.

sections.heading: Landing or missed approach
points: Section 91.175 requires the aircraft to be continuously in a position for a normal landing, flight visibility at least the published minimum and at least one specified visual reference before descent below minimums.

Start the published missed approach when required and advise ATC. If the missed approach begins before the missed approach point, continue on the final approach course until reaching it unless ATC directs otherwise.

numbers.value: Position, visibility and visual-reference tests must all be met
Approach lights alone allow descent only to 100 feet above touchdown-zone elevation

traps: Seeing approach lights does not automatically authorize descent to the runway.
A circling approach uses circling minimums and requires remaining within the protected area.

check.q: Which three conditions are required to descend below DA or MDA?
choices: Position, flight visibility and a listed visual reference
ATC approval, radar contact and landing clearance
check.why: Section 91.175(c) requires a normal-landing position, required flight visibility and at least one listed visual reference.

check.q: What is normally associated with a nonprecision approach?
check.why: Nonprecision procedures commonly use an MDA and a missed approach point.

check.q: What should a pilot verify after loading an approach into the navigator?
choices: The loaded procedure against the current chart
check.why: The pilot must catch database, selection or transition errors by comparing the loaded procedure with the chart.

modules.title: IFR weather, alternates and icing
modules.summary: Turn weather products into legal, conservative departure, enroute and approach decisions.

sections.heading: Weather planning
points: Build the picture from observations, forecasts, pilot reports, radar, satellite and advisories. Compare product valid times with the entire flight, not only departure.
Section 91.169 sets when an alternate is required and the forecast window around estimated arrival. Published alternate minimums or restrictions can replace the standard planning figures.

sections.heading: Icing and convective weather
points: Structural icing changes lift, drag, stall behavior and control response. Freezing rain and visible moisture near freezing demand wide margins and an exit plan.
Avoid thunderstorms rather than trying to penetrate cells visually or by airborne radar alone. Treat embedded convection, fast growth and strong echoes as reasons to reroute or land.

numbers.value: Destination, then alternate when required, then 45 minutes at normal cruise
1 hour before to 1 hour after estimated arrival
Less than 2,000-foot ceiling or 3 statute miles visibility

traps: The 1-2-3 rule decides whether to list an alternate; it does not set every alternate's filing minimums.
An icing forecast is not permission to fly an aircraft that lacks the required approval and capability.

check.q: After destination and required alternate fuel, what reserve does 91.167 require?
check.why: The IFR reserve is fuel for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed after reaching the alternate when one is required.

check.q: What does the 1-2-3 rule determine?
choices: Whether an alternate must be listed
Whether a VOR check is current
check.why: It uses forecast ceiling and visibility around arrival to determine whether the flight plan needs an alternate.

check.q: What is the safest basic response to an icing encounter?
check.why: Exit the icing conditions before performance and control degrade further.

modules.title: Emergencies, human factors and IFR decisions
modules.summary: Manage failures, workload and personal limits before they become an instrument emergency.
objectives: Use personal minimums and escape plans.

sections.heading: Failures and workload
points: Control the airplane, identify the failure, use the checklist and tell ATC what help is needed. Declare an emergency early when safety requires priority or flexibility.
Electrical, vacuum, pitot-static, navigation and communication failures create different cues. Rehearse each failure using the equipment installed in the airplane you fly.

sections.heading: Human performance and decisions
points: Instrument flight can create powerful vestibular illusions. Trust a verified instrument cross-check, not body sensations, and make deliberate changes.
Use personal minimums for ceiling, visibility, wind, icing and alternates. Reassess at decision points and keep a reachable route to better weather.

numbers.item: Hypoxia supplemental oxygen threshold for crew
numbers.value: More than 30 minutes above 12,500 feet MSL through 14,000 feet MSL

traps: Troubleshooting must not replace aircraft control.
Legal weather can still exceed a pilot's proficiency or the aircraft's practical capability.

library.q: emergencies spatial disorientation aeronautical decision making

check.q: What comes first after an instrument or system failure?
check.why: Aircraft control remains the first priority while the pilot identifies and manages the failure.

check.q: What should a pilot trust during spatial disorientation?
check.why: Vestibular sensations can be false in instrument conditions, so verified instruments provide the reliable reference.

check.q: Why set personal minimums before a flight?
choices: To make decisions before pressure rises
check.why: Predetermined limits reduce the temptation to rationalize a risky continuation under workload or schedule pressure.
